network.overall_strategy: We construct a comprehensive prebiotic synthesis network for threonine, tracing ten plausible pathways rooted in experimentally supported and literature-mandated geochemical scenarios. The dominant subnetworks are: (1) Strecker-type synthesis from C3 hydroxyaldehyde (lactaldehyde) derived via homologation and photoreduction of HCN/aldehyde substrates; (2) metal-chelate-catalyzed aldol-type condensations of glycine and acetaldehyde, producing β-hydroxy-α-amino acids; (3) 'shotgun' radical chemistry in atmospheric/surface discharge contexts; and (4) rare sugar-side product transformations via coupling and reduction. Intermediates are sourced by UV, photoreductive, mineral-catalyzed, or atmospheric processes. Hydrothermal routes are not supported, and biological analogues (homoserine pathway) remain hypothetical at best. The network reflects all documented limitations: low yields, lack of stereoselectivity, instability of threonine, and the central challenge posed by the availability of C2/C3 carbonyl intermediates. Each connection is justified by the cited literature or marked as speculative with chemical reasoning.

reactions.name: Formose reaction: HCN and formaldehyde to glycolaldehyde

conditions.other: neutral to mildly alkaline; wet-dry cycles

reactions.mechanism: Oligomerization of formaldehyde, catalyzed by minerals and cyanide, yields C2 sugars including glycolaldehyde.
reactions.reasoning: Formose chemistry yields glycolaldehyde in plausible surface settings (Weber & Miller, 1981; Patel et al., Nat. Chem. 2015). Montmorillonite and cyanide both promote this process.

reactions.name: Reduction of glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol
reactions.mechanism: Reductive conversion of glycolaldehyde to ethylene glycol on iron-sulfide in presence of H2S.
reactions.reasoning: Reduction demonstrated in cyanosulfidic sequences (Ritson & Sutherland, Angew. Chem. 2013).

reactions.name: Oxidation of ethylene glycol to glycolaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Photochemical oxidation provides recycling of glycolaldehyde from ethylene glycol.
reactions.reasoning: Surface UV allows bidirectional conversion between C2 alcohols and aldehydes, as observed in ice photolysis (Nuevo et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Homologation: Glycolaldehyde to glyceraldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Aldol addition of formaldehyde to glycolaldehyde forms glyceraldehyde; borate stabilizes sugar against decomposition.
reactions.reasoning: Borate promotes C3 sugar formation and selectivity (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013).

reactions.name: Reduction of glyceraldehyde to lactaldehyde
reactions.mechanism: Photoreduction of C3 sugar to hydroxypropanal via cyanosulfidic chemistry.
reactions.reasoning: Photoreduction demonstrated by Ritson & Sutherland (2013) and Patel et al. (2015); lactaldehyde forms as Strecker precursor.

reactions.name: Strecker reaction: lactaldehyde to threonine aminonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Imine formation between lactaldehyde and ammonia, followed by cyanide addition, gives 2-amino-3-hydroxybutanenitrile.
reactions.reasoning: Strecker pathway for threonine established; aminonitrile formation confirmed but not isolated yield (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of threonine aminonitrile to threonine and allothreonine

conditions.other: weakly acidic or hydrothermal, slow step

reactions.mechanism: Sequential hydrolysis of nitrile to amide and then carboxylic acid, yielding both threonine and allothreonine due to epimerization.
reactions.reasoning: Supported by classic Strecker/abiotic hydrolysis paths; lack of selectivity noted (Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Formose-access: glycolaldehyde and ammonia to glycine aminonitrile
reactions.mechanism: Strecker condensation on glycolaldehyde; further hydrolysis yields glycine.
reactions.reasoning: Standard Strecker; routine in meteorite models and experiments (Cobb & Pudritz 2015).

reactions.name: Hydrolysis of glycine aminonitrile to glycine
reactions.mechanism: Nitrile hydrolyzed to acid; hydrolysis assisted by clay/mineral and warm conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Routine in prebiotic models, also observed in parent body weathering (Cobb & Pudritz 2015).

reactions.name: Aldol-type condensation: glycine + acetaldehyde to threonine and allothreonine
reactions.mechanism: Cu(II)-glycinate complex enables nucleophilic addition to acetaldehyde; β-hydroxy amino acid forms; threo/allo ratio base-dependent.
reactions.reasoning: Documented experimentally (Sato et al., 1957; Weber & Miller 1981); high yield but metal/base loading not fully prebiotic.

reactions.name: Acetaldehyde formation by glycolaldehyde reduction
reactions.mechanism: Glycolaldehyde undergoes reductive deoxygenation to acetaldehyde under cyanosulfidic and photochemical conditions.
reactions.reasoning: Photoreduction confirmed in Sutherland’s cyanosulfidic network (Ritson & Sutherland, 2013; Patel et al., 2015).

reactions.name: Glycine + formaldehyde to serine by Strecker
reactions.mechanism: Glycine condenses via Strecker with formaldehyde and ammonia to yield serine.
reactions.reasoning: Observed as a major product in spark and ice-photolysis experiments (Ring et al., 1972; Nuevo et al., 2008).

reactions.name: Serine methylation to threonine (speculative)

conditions.other: requires simultaneous methyl source, little direct evidence

reactions.mechanism: Serine undergoes C-methylation at β-carbon by acetaldehyde, yielding threonine.
reactions.reasoning: Speculative; included as a plausible primitive methylation but unsupported in prebiotic setting. Provides network overlap.

reactions.name: Random radical/rainbow chemistry (shotgun) yields trace threonine
reactions.mechanism: Sulfur and radical chemistry on basic starting feedstock yields a complex mix of amino acids including threonine and allothreonine.
reactions.reasoning: Experimentally confirmed in H2S-rich Miller apparatus (Ring et al., 1972; Parker et al., 2011); only trace product, low selectivity.

pathways.name: Strecker from lactaldehyde
pathways.description: HCN and formaldehyde build successively to glycolaldehyde, glyceraldehyde, then photoreduction to lactaldehyde. Lactaldehyde undergoes Strecker aminonitrile formation and hydrolysis, giving threonine and allothreonine.

pathways.name: Aldol condensation of glycine and acetaldehyde (copper-catalyzed)
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde + ammonia + HCN gives glycine; glycolaldehyde is also photoreduced to acetaldehyde; glycine and acetaldehyde condense via Cu(II) catalysis to form threonine and allothreonine.

pathways.name: Shotgun discharge chemistry
pathways.description: Direct spark/radical chemistry on simple feedstocks in H2S-rich reducing atmosphere yields trace threonine (and allothreonine) with no selectivity.

pathways.name: Photoreductive pathway with ethylene glycol loop
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde is reduced to ethylene glycol, which is re-oxidized to glycolaldehyde, feeding into the Strecker or aldol routes; cycle allows regeneration under alternating redox surface conditions.

pathways.name: Strecker on sequential triose/hydroxypropanal
pathways.description: Glyceraldehyde, generated via formose-type chemistry, is photoreduced in the presence of HCN and ammonia to give directly lactaldehyde or other C3 hydroxy-aldehydes, which then undergo Strecker synthesis.

pathways.name: Serine methylation route (speculative)
pathways.description: Glycine and formaldehyde yield serine; serine is then C-methylated at the β carbon by acetaldehyde on clay or under UV, giving threonine.

pathways.name: Parallel Strecker/aldol split hub from glycolaldehyde
pathways.description: Network diversification from glycolaldehyde: one branch goes via aminonitrile to glycine, another to acetaldehyde, opening both Strecker and aldol routes to threonine, increasing possible product complexity.

pathways.name: Serine-centric pathway
pathways.description: Serine, generated via Strecker, is utilized as a hub for conversion to threonine (speculative or via trace radical chemistry), providing an alternative link between two networks.

pathways.name: Lactic acid side cycle (serine to lactic acid to lactaldehyde)
pathways.description: Serine undergoes deamination or dehydration to lactic acid; lactic acid is reduced to lactaldehyde, which undergoes the Strecker sequence to threonine.

pathways.name: Direct Strecker from glycolaldehyde + methylated imine (speculative)
pathways.description: Glycolaldehyde reacts with ammonia and cyanide to yield glycine aminonitrile; spontaneous methylation or addition with acetaldehyde generates threonine aminonitrile or threonine directly upon hydrolysis.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The Strecker-type synthesis from lactaldehyde is fully expected as a literature-rooted route, but reaction balance checks reveal major flaws in several steps (notably rxn_001, rxn_006, rxn_007). The formation of lactaldehyde is supported, but all Strecker reactions here omit water as a key product or are missing balancing details. Hydrolysis to threonine and allothreonine is particularly problematic (rxn_007 is not balanceable and omits water/ammonia). Conditions are plausible (surface, UV, mineral catalysis), but in practice, yields are trace and selective product isolation is unrealistic. This pathway presents a representative, but not strictly valid, surface chemistry strategy.
suggestions: Explicitly include all stoichiometric water/ammonia in Strecker and hydrolysis steps.
Clarify reaction coefficients or intermediate pools, especially for aminonitrile hydrolysis.
Recheck formula and mass balance for each step.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This aldol condensation route is rooted in known Akabori/metal-catalyzed chemistry, but several reactions are unbalanced (notably rxn_011—glycolaldehyde to acetaldehyde, and rxn_007—aminonitrile hydrolysis), and preparative yields are not plausible in prebiotic conditions. Metal ions (Cu/Co) are appropriate in this context, but the actual process would likely favor retro-aldol reactions, reducing net product. Also, the hydrolysis step to threonine and allothreonine remains chemically and stoichiometrically problematic.
suggestions: Balance all aldol and amination reactions with proper stoichiometry.
Include water or co-products where physically necessary.
Align intermediates with literature yield limits and reversibility.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The 'shotgun' radical/discharge pathway (rxn_014) aligns closely with the only demonstrated direct prebiotic production of threonine—very low yield, nonselective, but verified in Miller–Urey and other discharge experiments. While yield is extremely poor and selectivity is absent, the overall chemistry is plausible and supported by experimental results. Atom balance is approximate, but such steps are understood to be summary representations.
suggestions: Specify yields (trace), and note 1:1 threo:allo ratio.
Clarify that this step abstracts complex, unbalanced radical chemistry but is justified by experiment.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Photoreductive and aldol-homologation steps (rxn_002, rxn_003) are plausible and rooted in recent experimental advances, but atom balance is not validated for key intermediates and the core Strecker/hydrolysis reactions suffer the same stoichiometric issues as in P1. This is a conceptually valuable pathway but its component chemistry must be rendered fully balanced for approval.
suggestions: Correct atom/charge balance for C2/C3 homologations and Strecker-derived steps.
Link all co-products.
Document sub-dominant yield in commentary.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway combines triose and hydroxypropanal Strecker chemistry, also supported by cyanosulfidic literature, but suffers all of the mass/charge balance issues that affect aminonitrile and hydrolysis steps (rxn_004, rxn_005, rxn_006, rxn_007, rxn_008). Literature supports this as a possible minor route; network-level accounting requires reaction balance fixes.
suggestions: Full atom/charge balance in all steps.
Clarify all products and include stoichiometric water release.
Align with demonstrated aminonitrile intermediacy.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Serine methylation (rxn_013) is speculative and not demonstrated in abiotic systems; atom balance fails for key steps (rxn_012, rxn_013, rxn_007). This pathway is not supported by nonenzymatic experimental evidence. If it were to be retained, it should be explicitly marked as hypothetical and removed from main production estimates.
suggestions: Remove or clearly demarcate as speculative/hypothetical.
Route serine methylation via plausible plausible prebiotic chemistry only if available.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This pathway explores parallel Strecker/aldol access to threonine via glycolaldehyde. Again, several reactions are unbalanced (rxn_001, rxn_008, rxn_009, rxn_011), and mechanistic details (e.g., hydrolytic steps) are not tracked. The concept is plausible but stoichiometry must be repaired.
suggestions: Complete balancing of all steps.
Clarify any ambiguous intermediate transformations.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: Serine-centric routes lack literature support for the proposed serine methylation, which is not a demonstrated or plausible prebiotic route; chemical and atom/charge balance issues are present (rxn_012, rxn_013, rxn_011). This pathway should be relegated to speculative status.
suggestions: Remove as standard route or make purely hypothetical.
Support with referenced abiotic chemistry if ever possible.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: The lactic acid and serine side cycle route is speculative for most steps beyond lactic acid/serine interconversion, and the critical serine methylation is not plausible prebiotically as currently formulated (rxn_013 problematic). Atom/charge balance is missing for hydrolysis and methylation events.
suggestions: Restrict to better-supported, compartmentalized chemistry.
Correct all stoichiometry and mechanistic details.

pathway_evaluations.feedback: This speculative direct Strecker from glycolaldehyde via methylated imine lacks experimental precedent, and key steps (rxn_006, rxn_007, rxn_001) are not valid in mass balance or mechanistic detail. As currently written, represents a chemically creative but not demonstrated network.
suggestions: Remove unless mechanistic support can be documented.
Balance all Strecker/hydrolysis reactions.

evaluation.network_feedback: This threonine synthesis network is comprehensive in scope and covers all plausible and speculative prebiotic scenarios reported in the literature, accurately reflecting the extreme scarcity and instability of threonine as an abiotic product. Pathway topology is representative and does not omit any known minor or major route. However, the network is critically hampered by widespread mass and charge conservation violations in core steps, particularly every Strecker, aminonitrile hydrolysis, and serine methylation event. Several reactions omit required water/ammonia byproducts or use intermediates with formula inconsistencies. The strongest, best-supported routes (shotgun discharge—P3; Strecker—P1/P4; aldol—P2) are present but must be rendered strictly stoichiometric. Environmental assignments are generally appropriate, with surface/UV/radical chemistry reflecting conditions where trace threonine is known to form. Literature alignment is solid: the network is honest about diastereoselectivity issues, low yields, analytical caveats, and instability. However, major corrections to reaction stoichiometry and balancing are needed to meet validity and chemical feasibility standards. With these improvements, and removal or explicit disclaimer of speculative/methylation routes, the network would be ready for approval.
